questions.question: The function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ defined by $f(n)=2n+3$ is
questions.answer:
**(A)** one-one

**Test injectivity.** Suppose $f(n_1)=f(n_2)$:
$$2n_1+3=2n_2+3\ \Rightarrow\ 2n_1=2n_2\ \Rightarrow\ n_1=n_2$$

Distinct inputs give distinct outputs, so $f$ is **one-one**.

**Test surjectivity.** The smallest codomain element is $1\in\mathbb{N}$; try to hit it:
$$2n+3=1\ \Rightarrow\ n=-1\notin\mathbb{N}$$

So $1$ has no preimage and $f$ is **not onto**. In fact $f(n)\ge2(1)+3=5$, so $1,2,3,4$ are never attained.

$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is one-one but not onto}$$

**Image set:** $f(\mathbb{N})=\{5,7,9,11,\dots\}$, a proper subset of $\mathbb{N}$ — injective without being surjective.

questions.question: If $f:\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}$ is given by $f(x)=x^{2}$ then $f^{-1}(9)=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\pm3$

To invert, put $y=f(x)$ and solve for $x$:
$$y=x^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ x=\pm\sqrt y$$

With $y=9$:
$$x=\pm\sqrt9=\pm3$$

$$\therefore\ f^{-1}(9)=\pm3$$

**Both values are legitimate** because $f(x)=x^{2}$ on $\mathbb{Q}$ is **not** one-one: both $3$ and $-3$ map to $9$, so the inverse relation is two-valued.

**Remark:** strictly, this $f$ has no inverse *function* (it is many-one), only an inverse *relation*. The question uses the school convention $f^{-1}(y)=\{x:f(x)=y\}$, which is why the two-valued answer is accepted. Had the domain been restricted to $[0,\infty)$, the answer would be $+3$ alone.

questions.question: The principal value of $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(-\sqrt2\right)$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

The principal branch of $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}$ is $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\setminus\{0\}$. We need the angle there whose cosecant is $-\sqrt2$.

$$\operatorname{cosec}\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{\sin(-\pi/4)}=\frac{1}{-1/\sqrt2}=-\sqrt2,\qquad -\frac{\pi}{4}\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\ ✓$$

$$\therefore\ \operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(-\sqrt2\right)=-\frac{\pi}{4}$$

**Equivalently**, $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}(-x)=-\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x$, so
$$\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(-\sqrt2\right)=-\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}\left(\sqrt2\right)=-\frac{\pi}{4}\ ✓$$

**Why $-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ is rejected:** although $\operatorname{cosec}\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)=-\sqrt2$, that angle lies outside $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, so it is not the principal value.

questions.question: If $\begin{bmatrix}x+y+z\\ x+z\\ y+z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}9\\ 5\\ 7\end{bmatrix}$ then $x+y+z=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $9$

Comparing corresponding entries of the two column vectors:
$$x+y+z=9\qquad\ldots(1)$$
$$x+z=5\qquad\ldots(2)$$
$$y+z=7\qquad\ldots(3)$$

**The answer is already in (1):** the first component of the left vector *is* the required sum, so
$$x+y+z=9$$

**Check by solving.** Add (2) and (3): $x+y+2z=12$; subtract (1): $z=3$. Then $x=5-3=2$ and $y=7-3=4$, giving $x+y+z=2+4+3=9$ ✓ — consistent.

questions.question: Matrices $A$ and $B$ are invertible of each other iff
questions.answer:
**(D)** $AB=BA=I$

Two square matrices of the same order are inverses of each other when their products in both orders equal the identity:
$$AB=BA=I$$

$$\therefore\ B=A^{-1}\ \text{and}\ A=B^{-1}$$

**Why both orders?** $B$ is a right inverse if $AB=I$ and a left inverse if $BA=I$. For square matrices over a field one condition forces the other — which is why the determinant test works: $AB=I\Rightarrow|A||B|=1\Rightarrow|A|\neq0$. The question states the full condition, so (D) is exact.

**Why the others fail:** $AB=BA$ alone only says the matrices *commute* (e.g. $A=B=I$); $AB=BA=0$ describes orthogonal annihilation (both singular); and $AB=0,\ BA=I$ is self-contradictory, since $BA=I$ forces both factors nonsingular, hence $AB\neq0$.

questions.question: $\begin{vmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{vmatrix}=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $1$

This is the identity matrix $I_3$. Expanding along the first row:
$$\begin{vmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{vmatrix}-0+0=1(1-0)=1$$

More simply, the matrix is **triangular** (diagonal), so its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries:
$$|I_3|=1\times1\times1=1$$

$$\therefore\ \text{determinant}=1$$

**Consistency:** $|I_n|=1$ for every $n$ — the identity map leaves volumes unchanged, and the determinant measures volume scaling. Option (C) '3' is the *trace*, not the determinant.

questions.question: Co-factor of $(-3)$ in $\begin{vmatrix}0&1&-2\\ -1&0&2\\ 2&-3&0\end{vmatrix}$ is
questions.answer:
**(D)** none of these — the cofactor is $2$

The entry $-3$ is in **row 3, column 2**. Delete row 3 and column 2 to get the minor:
$$M_{32}=\begin{vmatrix}0&-2\\ -1&2\end{vmatrix}=0(2)-(-2)(-1)=0-2=-2$$

The cofactor carries the sign $(-1)^{3+2}=-1$:
$$C_{32}=(-1)^{3+2}M_{32}=(-1)(-2)=2$$

$$\therefore\ \text{cofactor of }(-3)=2$$

Since $2$ is not among $1,-1,0$, the answer is **'none of these'**.

**The usual trap** is to report the minor $-2$ (forgetting the sign) or to take $(-1)^{3+2}$ as $+1$ — both give $-2$ and neither gives the correct $2$.

questions.question: If $y=2^{x}$ then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $2^{x}\left(\log2\right)$

Write the exponential with base $e$:
$$2^{x}=e^{x\log2}$$

Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{kx}=ke^{kx}$ with $k=\log2$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\left(\log2\right)e^{x\log2}=2^{x}\log2$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=2^{x}\log2$$

**General rule:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^{x}=a^{x}\log a$ — the factor is multiplied, **not** divided (dividing would be the antiderivative rule).

**Check by logarithmic differentiation:** $\log y=x\log2\Rightarrow\dfrac1y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\log2\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2^{x}\log2$ ✓.

**Option (1) warning:** $x2^{x-1}$ is the derivative of $x^{2}$, not of $2^{x}$ — variable and base have been swapped.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}2x=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{1-4x^{2}}}$

Chain rule with $u=2x$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}$$

Here $\dfrac{du}{dx}=2$ and $u^{2}=4x^{2}$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}2x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4x^{2}}}\cdot2=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-4x^{2}}}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}2x=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-4x^{2}}}\qquad\left(|x|<\frac12\right)$$

**Check near $x=0$:** $\sin^{-1}2x\approx2x$, whose slope is $2$ — and the formula gives $\dfrac{2}{1}=2$ at $x=0$ ✓. Option (1) multiplies by $2x$ instead of $2$, confusing the inner function with its derivative.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log\left(\sin x\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\cot x$

Chain rule with the outer function $\log$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\log\left(\sin x\right)=\frac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sin x\right)=\frac{1}{\sin x}\cdot\cos x$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}\log\left(\sin x\right)=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}=\cot x$$

**Validity:** needs $\sin x>0$ (logarithm) and $\sin x\neq0$ (division); both hold on $\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

**Numerical check** at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$: $\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=1$, and the function $\log(\sin x)$ does have slope $1$ there ✓.

The related integral identity $\displaystyle\int\cot x\,dx=\log\left|\sin x\right|+C$ is this derivative read backwards.

questions.question: If $x=4t$, $y=\dfrac4t$ then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $-\dfrac{1}{t^{2}}$

**Step 1 — differentiate each variable with respect to $t$:**
$$\frac{dx}{dt}=4,\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac{4}{t^{2}}$$

**Step 2 — divide:**
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\frac{-4/t^{2}}{4}=-\frac{1}{t^{2}}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{t^{2}}$$

**Alternative check without the parameter:** from $x=4t$, $t=\dfrac x4$, so $y=\dfrac{4}{x/4}=\dfrac{16}{x}$ and
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{16}{x^{2}}=-\frac{16}{16t^{2}}=-\frac{1}{t^{2}}\ ✓$$

The curve is the rectangular hyperbola $xy=16$, whose slope is negative for $t>0$ ✓.

questions.question: If $y=\log x$ then $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{-1}{x^{2}}$

**First derivative:**
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac1x=x^{-1}$$

**Second derivative:**
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=(-1)x^{-2}=-\frac{1}{x^{2}}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\qquad(x>0)$$

**Interpretation:** $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac1x>0$, so $\log x$ is increasing; but the slope $\dfrac1x$ decreases with $x$, so the graph is concave down everywhere — exactly what the negative second derivative says ✓.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{x^{11}}\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{-1}{10x^{10}}+c$

Write the integrand as a power and use $\displaystyle\int x^{n}dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$ with $n=-11\neq-1$:
$$\int x^{-11}dx=\frac{x^{-10}}{-10}=-\frac{1}{10x^{10}}+c$$

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{dx}{x^{11}}=-\frac{1}{10x^{10}}+c$$

**Check by differentiating:**
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(-\frac{1}{10}x^{-10}\right)=-\frac{1}{10}(-10)x^{-11}=x^{-11}=\frac{1}{x^{11}}\ ✓$$

**Caution:** the exponent is $-11$, not $-1$; for $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x}$ the answer would be $\log|x|+c$. Option (3) mistakes the reciprocal of the new exponent for the exponent itself.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\sin^{2}x\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac x2-\dfrac{\sin2x}{4}+c$

**Step 1 — linearise** with $\sin^{2}x=\dfrac{1-\cos2x}{2}$:
$$\int\sin^{2}x\,dx=\frac12\int\left(1-\cos2x\right)dx$$

**Step 2 — integrate** (using $\displaystyle\int\cos2x\,dx=\frac{\sin2x}{2}$):
$$=\frac12\left[x-\frac{\sin2x}{2}\right]+c=\frac x2-\frac{\sin2x}{4}+c$$

$$\therefore\ \int\sin^{2}x\,dx=\frac x2-\frac{\sin2x}{4}+c$$

**Check by differentiating:**
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac x2-\frac{\sin2x}{4}\right]=\frac12-\frac{2\cos2x}{4}=\frac{1-\cos2x}{2}=\sin^{2}x\ ✓$$

**Sanity check:** the integrand is non-negative, so the integral must be increasing; the formula gives derivative $\sin^2 x\ge0$ ✓ (it is zero exactly at multiples of $\pi$).

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{4+x^{2}}\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\dfrac12\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac x2\right)+c$

Use $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{a^{2}+x^{2}}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac xa+c$ with $a^{2}=4$, i.e. $a=2$:
$$\int\frac{dx}{4+x^{2}}=\frac12\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x2\right)+c$$

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{dx}{4+x^{2}}=\frac12\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x2\right)+c$$

**By substitution** ($x=2\tan\theta$, $dx=2\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta$):
$$\int\frac{2\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta}{4+4\tan^{2}\theta}=\int\frac{2\sec^{2}\theta}{4\sec^{2}\theta}d\theta=\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac x2\ ✓$$

**Check by differentiating:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac12\tan^{-1}\dfrac x2\right]=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+x^{2}/4}\cdot\dfrac12=\dfrac{1}{4+x^{2}}$ ✓. Option (1) omits the factor $\dfrac1a$; option (3) uses $a=3$ by mistake.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{3}\frac1x\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\log\left(\dfrac32\right)$

An antiderivative of $\dfrac1x$ is $\log x$:
$$\int_{2}^{3}\frac{dx}{x}=\left[\log x\right]_{2}^{3}=\log3-\log2=\log\frac32$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{2}^{3}\frac{dx}{x}=\log\frac32\approx0.405$$

**Size check:** on $[2,3]$ the integrand falls from $\dfrac12$ to $\dfrac13$, so the integral lies between $\dfrac13\approx0.333$ and $\dfrac12=0.5$. Indeed $\log1.5\approx0.405$ ✓.

**Sign check:** the limits are in increasing order and the integrand is positive, so the answer must be **positive** — option (C) $\log\dfrac23\approx-0.405$ comes from reversing the limits and is wrong.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

The antiderivative is $\sin^{-1}x$:
$$\int_{0}^{1}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}=\left[\sin^{-1}x\right]_{0}^{1}=\sin^{-1}1-\sin^{-1}0=\frac{\pi}{2}-0$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{0}^{1}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}=\frac{\pi}{2}$$

**Angle reading:** the integrand is the derivative of $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$; as $x$ goes from $0$ to $1$ the angle goes from $0$ to $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so the integral is the total angle change ✓.

**Note:** the integrand blows up as $x\to1^{-}$ (vertical tangent of the circle), yet the integral is finite — an improper integral that converges because $\sin^{-1}$ is continuous at $1$.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a}f(x)\,dx=0$ if
questions.answer:
**(C)** $f(2a-x)=-f(x)$

Let $I=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a}f(x)\,dx$ and substitute $x=2a-t$, so $dx=-dt$; when $x=0$, $t=2a$ and when $x=2a$, $t=0$:
$$I=\int_{2a}^{0}f(2a-t)(-dt)=\int_{0}^{2a}f(2a-t)\,dt=\int_{0}^{2a}f(2a-x)\,dx$$

If $f(2a-x)=-f(x)$, this reads
$$I=-\int_{0}^{2a}f(x)\,dx=-I\ \Rightarrow\ 2I=0\ \Rightarrow\ I=0$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{0}^{2a}f(x)\,dx=0\quad\text{when }f(2a-x)=-f(x)$$

**Why the other options fail.** Option (A) 'even' concerns symmetry about $0$, not about $a$. Option (B) gives $I=I$ — an identity true for *every* integrable $f$, so it cannot force $I=0$. Option (D) is the classic trap: an odd function gives $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=0$, a symmetric interval about the **origin**, not $[0,2a]$. For instance $f(x)=x$ is odd yet $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a}x\,dx=2a^{2}\neq0$.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet marks (D). That is **wrong** for the reason just given; the correct condition is (C), the symmetry about the midpoint $x=a$.

**Example confirming (C):** take $a=1$, $f(x)=x-1$. Then $f(2-x)=1-x=-f(x)$ ✓ and
$$\int_{0}^{2}(x-1)\,dx=\left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}-x\right]_{0}^{2}=2-2=0\ ✓

questions.question: General solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac yx$ is
questions.answer:
**(A)** $y=cx$

Separate the variables:
$$\frac{dy}{y}=\frac{dx}{x}$$

Integrate, writing the constant as $\log|c|$:
$$\log|y|=\log|x|+\log|c|=\log|cx|$$
$$y=cx$$

$$\therefore\ y=cx$$

**Interpretation:** the equation says the slope at every point equals $\dfrac yx$, i.e. the tangent at each point passes through the origin — precisely the property of lines through the origin, so the general solution is the pencil $y=cx$ ✓.

**Check:** with $y=cx$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=c=\dfrac{cx}{x}=\dfrac yx$ ✓. (Option (B) is the same family with $c$ relabelled as $\dfrac1c$.)

questions.question: The integrating factor of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}-y=\cos x$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $e^{-x}$

The equation is already in the standard form $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q$ with
$$P=-1,\qquad Q=\cos x$$

$$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int P\,dx}=e^{\int(-1)dx}=e^{-x}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{I.F.}=e^{-x}$$

**Verification that it works:** multiplying through by $e^{-x}$,
$$e^{-x}\frac{dy}{dx}-e^{-x}y=e^{-x}\cos x\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{-x}\right)=e^{-x}\cos x$$
so the left side is exactly the derivative of $y\times\text{I.F.}$ ✓ — the defining property.

**Solving on:** $ye^{-x}=\displaystyle\int e^{-x}\cos x\,dx=\frac{e^{-x}}{2}\left(\sin x-\cos x\right)+C$, giving $y=\dfrac{\sin x-\cos x}{2}+Ce^{x}$.

questions.question: Unit vector of $\vec a$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\dfrac{\vec a}{\left|\vec a\right|}$

A unit vector along $\vec a$ is the *vector* divided by its magnitude:
$$\hat a=\frac{\vec a}{\left|\vec a\right|}\qquad(\vec a\neq\vec 0)$$

$$\therefore\ \hat a=\frac{\vec a}{\left|\vec a\right|}$$

**Why it is a unit vector:**
$$\left|\hat a\right|=\frac{\left|\vec a\right|}{\left|\vec a\right|}=1\ ✓$$

**Component check:** for $\vec a=3\hat i+4\hat j$, $\left|\vec a\right|=5$ and $\hat a=\dfrac35\hat i+\dfrac45\hat j$ with magnitude $\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}+\frac{16}{25}}=1$ ✓.

**Options (A) and (C) are scalars:** $a$ without an arrow is a number, and so is $1$; neither is a vector, hence neither can be a unit vector.

questions.question: Projection of $\hat i$ on $\hat j$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $0$

The scalar projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$ is $\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{\left|\vec b\right|}$.

Here $\vec a=\hat i$, $\vec b=\hat j$ and $\hat i\cdot\hat j=0$, because the unit vectors along perpendicular axes are orthogonal:
$$\text{projection}=\frac{0}{1}=0$$

$$\therefore\ \text{projection of }\hat i\text{ on }\hat j=0$$

**Geometric meaning:** the shadow of a unit vector along the $x$-axis, cast on the $y$-axis, has zero length — the two directions are at $90^{\circ}$, and $\cos90^{\circ}=0$ ✓.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet marks (A) $1$. That is **wrong** — $1$ is the projection of $\hat i$ on **itself** ($\hat i\cdot\hat i=1$), not on the perpendicular direction $\hat j$.

questions.question: If $\vec a\cdot\vec b=1$, $\left|\vec a\right|=1$ and $\left|\vec b\right|=2$ then $\cos\theta=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\dfrac12$

By definition of the dot product,
$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=\left|\vec a\right|\left|\vec b\right|\cos\theta$$
$$1=(1)(2)\cos\theta=2\cos\theta$$
$$\cos\theta=\frac12$$

$$\therefore\ \cos\theta=\frac12\ \Rightarrow\ \theta=60^{\circ}$$

**Admissibility:** $\dfrac12\in[-1,1]$ ✓, so a genuine angle exists.

**Scale check:** the largest dot product these magnitudes allow is $1\times2=2$ (at $\theta=0$); the given value $1$ is exactly half of that, matching $\cos\theta=\dfrac12$ ✓.

questions.question: $\hat k\times\hat j=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $-\hat i$

For the right-handed system,
$$\hat i\times\hat j=\hat k,\qquad \hat j\times\hat k=\hat i,\qquad \hat k\times\hat i=\hat j$$

Reversing any order flips the sign, so
$$\hat k\times\hat j=-\left(\hat j\times\hat k\right)=-\hat i$$

$$\therefore\ \hat k\times\hat j=-\hat i$$

**Determinant check:**
$$\hat k\times\hat j=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\end{vmatrix}=\hat i(0-1)-\hat j(0-0)+\hat k(0-0)=-\hat i\ ✓$$

**Right-hand rule:** curling the fingers from the $z$-axis towards the $y$-axis makes the thumb point along the negative $x$-axis ✓.

questions.question: The direction ratio of the line $\dfrac x1=\dfrac y1=\dfrac z1$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $1,1,1$

For a line $\dfrac{x-x_{1}}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_{1}}{b}=\dfrac{z-z_{1}}{c}$, the **direction ratios** are the denominators $(a,b,c)$.

Here $a=b=c=1$, so
$$\therefore\ \text{direction ratios}=(1,1,1)$$

**Ratios versus cosines.** Dividing by the magnitude $\sqrt{1+1+1}=\sqrt3$ gives the **direction cosines** $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$ — that is option (A). The question asks for ratios, so (B) is right.

**Quick eliminations:** $(0,0,0)$ gives no direction at all (impossible), and the triple with $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ has squared sum $\dfrac32\neq1$, so it is not a valid cosine triple either.

questions.question: Equation of $x$-axis is
questions.answer:
**(A)** $y=0,\ z=0$

The $x$-axis is the set of points whose $y$- and $z$-coordinates vanish while $x$ is free:
$$\{(x,0,0):x\in\mathbb{R}\}$$
$$y=0\quad\text{and}\quad z=0$$

$$\therefore\ \text{equation of the }x\text{-axis: }y=0,\ z=0$$

**Identifying the others:** (B) $x=0,y=0$ is the $z$-axis; (C) $x=0,z=0$ is the $y$-axis; (D) $x=y=z=0$ is the single point $O$, not a line.

**Symmetric form:** the $x$-axis is $\dfrac{x}{1}=\dfrac{y}{0}=\dfrac{z}{0}$, direction ratios $(1,0,0)$ — consistent with $y$ and $z$ frozen at zero.

questions.question: If the lines $\dfrac{x-2}{1}=\dfrac{y-3}{1}=\dfrac{z-4}{k}$ and $\dfrac{x-1}{k}=\dfrac{y-4}{2}=\dfrac{z-5}{-2}$ are mutually perpendicular, then $k$ is
questions.answer:
**(D)** $2$

**Step 1 — direction ratios.**
$$\vec b_{1}=(1,\ 1,\ k),\qquad \vec b_{2}=(k,\ 2,\ -2)$$

**Step 2 — perpendicular lines have perpendicular directions:**
$$\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}=0$$
$$(1)(k)+(1)(2)+(k)(-2)=0$$
$$k+2-2k=0\ \Rightarrow\ 2-k=0\ \Rightarrow\ k=2$$

$$\therefore\ k=2$$

**Check:** with $k=2$ the directions are $(1,1,2)$ and $(2,2,-2)=2(1,1,-1)$; and $(1,1,2)\cdot(1,1,-1)=1+1-2=0$ ✓.

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet marks (A) $-\dfrac23$, which comes from a sign slip in the third product (using $+2k$ instead of $-2k$). Solving the printed condition correctly gives $k=2$, option (D).

questions.question: The distance of the point $P(a,b,c)$ from the $x$-axis is
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}}$

The foot of the perpendicular from $P(a,b,c)$ on the $x$-axis is $Q(a,0,0)$ — same $x$, with $y=z=0$. Hence
$$PQ=\sqrt{(a-a)^{2}+(b-0)^{2}+(c-0)^{2}}=\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{distance from the }x\text{-axis}=\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}}$$

**Pattern:** the distance to an axis uses the two coordinates *perpendicular* to it —
- from the $x$-axis: $\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}}$
- from the $y$-axis: $\sqrt{a^{2}+c^{2}}$ (option B)
- from the $z$-axis: $\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ (option C)

**Check:** for $P(3,4,12)$ the distance from the $x$-axis is $\sqrt{16+144}=4\sqrt{10}\approx12.65$, while $\left|OP\right|=13$ — the axis distance is smaller, as it must be ✓.

questions.question: If $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{7}{10}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac{17}{20}$ then $P\left(\dfrac AB\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{14}{17}$

By definition,
$$P\left(\frac AB\right)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{7/10}{17/20}$$

Rewrite as a product and cancel:
$$=\frac{7}{10}\times\frac{20}{17}=\frac{7\times2}{17}=\frac{14}{17}$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac AB\right)=\frac{14}{17}\approx0.824$$

**Data check:** we need $P(A\cap B)\le P(B)$, i.e. $\dfrac{14}{20}\le\dfrac{17}{20}$ ✓. The conditional value $\dfrac{14}{17}$ is a fraction of $B$'s probability, hence at most $1$ ✓.

questions.question: If the events $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $P(A\cap B)=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $P(A)\cdot P(B)$

Independence means the occurrence of one event does not change the probability of the other:
$$P\left(\frac AB\right)=P(A)$$

Substituting $P(A/B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$ and multiplying by $P(B)$:
$$P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)$$

$$\therefore\ P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)$$

**Worked example:** two fair coins. $P(\text{first head})=\dfrac12$, $P(\text{second head})=\dfrac12$, and $P(\text{both})=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac12=\dfrac14$ — matching the direct count of $1$ favourable case out of $4$ ✓.

**Keep these three apart:**
- independent: $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$
- mutually exclusive: $P(A\cap B)=0$
- always: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$

questions.question: Let $f$ be an invertible real function. Find the value of $\left(f^{-1}\circ f\right)(1)+\left(f^{-1}\circ f\right)(2)+\left(f^{-1}\circ f\right)(3)+\left(f^{-1}\circ f\right)(4)$.
questions.answer:
For an invertible function, composing with the inverse returns the input:
$$\left(f^{-1}\circ f\right)(x)=f^{-1}\left(f(x)\right)=x$$

So each term equals its own argument:
$$\left(f^{-1}\circ f\right)(1)=1,\quad \left(f^{-1}\circ f\right)(2)=2,\quad \left(f^{-1}\circ f\right)(3)=3,\quad \left(f^{-1}\circ f\right)(4)=4$$

Adding:
$$1+2+3+4=10$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the required sum}=10$$

**General fact:** $f^{-1}\circ f=I$ on the domain of $f$ and $f\circ f^{-1}=I$ on its codomain — the two identities that make $f^{-1}$ the inverse. The sum is then $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{4}k=\frac{4\cdot5}{2}=10$.

questions.question: Prove that $\tan^{-1}\dfrac17+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{13}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac29$.
questions.answer:
Use the addition formula
$$\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\qquad(xy<1)$$

with $x=\dfrac17$, $y=\dfrac1{13}$. Here $xy=\dfrac{1}{91}<1$, so no adjustment by $\pi$ is needed.

**Numerator:**
$$x+y=\frac17+\frac{1}{13}=\frac{13+7}{91}=\frac{20}{91}$$

**Denominator:**
$$1-xy=1-\frac{1}{91}=\frac{90}{91}$$

**Divide:**
$$\frac{x+y}{1-xy}=\frac{20/91}{90/91}=\frac{20}{90}=\frac29$$

$$\therefore\ \tan^{-1}\frac17+\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{13}=\tan^{-1}\frac29\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Numerical check:** $\tan^{-1}\dfrac17\approx8.13^{\circ}$ and $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{13}\approx4.40^{\circ}$, sum $\approx12.53^{\circ}$; and $\tan^{-1}\dfrac29\approx12.53^{\circ}$ ✓.

questions.question: If $y=x^{\cos x}$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
questions.answer:
The variable occurs in **both** the base and the exponent, so take logarithms.

**Step 1 — take $\log$:**
$$\log y=\cos x\cdot\log x$$

**Step 2 — differentiate both sides** (product rule on the right):
$$\frac1y\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos x\cdot\frac1x+\left(-\sin x\right)\log x$$

**Step 3 — multiply by $y$, restoring $y=x^{\cos x}$:**
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=x^{\cos x}\left[\frac{\cos x}{x}-\sin x\,\log x\right]$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=x^{\cos x}\left[\frac{\cos x}{x}-\sin x\,\log x\right]$$

**Validity:** this needs $x>0$, so that $\log x$ and the real power $x^{\cos x}=e^{\cos x\log x}$ both make sense.

**Check at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:** there $\cos x=0$, so $y=1$, and the bracket becomes $0-\left(1\right)\log\dfrac{\pi}{2}=-\log\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ — a small negative slope, consistent with $x^{\cos x}$ dipping just below $1$ near $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ ✓.

questions.question: If the points $(5,5)$, $(k,1)$ and $(10,7)$ are collinear, find the value of $k$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — collinearity means zero area**, i.e. the determinant of the coordinates vanishes:
$$\begin{vmatrix}5&5&1\\ k&1&1\\ 10&7&1\end{vmatrix}=0$$

**Step 2 — expand along the first row:**
$$5\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\ 7&1\end{vmatrix}-5\begin{vmatrix}k&1\\ 10&1\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}k&1\\ 10&7\end{vmatrix}=0$$

$$5(1-7)-5(k-10)+(7k-10)=0$$

$$-30-5k+50+7k-10=0$$

**Step 3 — simplify:**
$$2k+10=0\ \Rightarrow\ k=-5$$

$$\therefore\ k=-5$$

**Check by slopes** (an independent route): the slope from $(5,5)$ to $(10,7)$ is
$$\frac{7-5}{10-5}=\frac25$$
The slope from $(5,5)$ to $(k,1)=(-5,1)$ is
$$\frac{1-5}{-5-5}=\frac{-4}{-10}=\frac25\ ✓$$
equal, so the three points are collinear.

questions.topic: Second Derivative of a Trigonometric Combination
questions.question: If $y=A\sin x+B\cos x$, then prove that $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+y=0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — first derivative:**
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=A\cos x-B\sin x$$

**Step 2 — second derivative:**
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-A\sin x-B\cos x$$

**Step 3 — recognise the original function:**
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-\left(A\sin x+B\cos x\right)=-y$$

Hence
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+y=-y+y=0\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Meaning:** $y=A\sin x+B\cos x$ is the general solution of the simple harmonic equation $y''+y=0$ — every such combination is its own negative second derivative, which is exactly why sines and cosines describe oscillations.

**Check with numbers:** take $A=1$, $B=0$, $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$. Then $y=\dfrac12$ and $y''=-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}=-\dfrac12$, so $y''+y=-\dfrac12+\dfrac12=0$ ✓.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int\frac{x\tan^{-1}x^{2}}{1+x^{4}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — spot that the derivative of $\tan^{-1}x^{2}$ appears in the numerator.** Let
$$t=\tan^{-1}x^{2}$$

Then
$$\frac{dt}{dx}=\frac{1}{1+\left(x^{2}\right)^{2}}\cdot2x=\frac{2x}{1+x^{4}}$$
so
$$dt=\frac{2x\,dx}{1+x^{4}}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{x\,dx}{1+x^{4}}=\frac{dt}{2}$$

**Step 2 — substitute:**
$$\int\frac{x\tan^{-1}x^{2}}{1+x^{4}}dx=\int t\cdot\frac{dt}{2}=\frac12\cdot\frac{t^{2}}{2}+C=\frac{t^{2}}{4}+C$$

**Step 3 — restore $t$:**
$$\therefore\ \int\frac{x\tan^{-1}x^{2}}{1+x^{4}}\,dx=\frac{1}{4}\left(\tan^{-1}x^{2}\right)^{2}+C$$

**Check by differentiating:**
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac14\left(\tan^{-1}x^{2}\right)^{2}\right]=\frac14\cdot2\left(\tan^{-1}x^{2}\right)\cdot\frac{2x}{1+x^{4}}=\frac{x\tan^{-1}x^{2}}{1+x^{4}}\ ✓$$

questions.question: Two coins are tossed once. Find $P\left(\dfrac EF\right)$ where $E$ = no tail appears and $F$ = no head appears.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the sample space.** With two coins, $2^{2}=4$ equally likely outcomes:
$$S=\{HH,\ HT,\ TH,\ TT\},\qquad n(S)=4$$

**Step 2 — the event $E$** (no tail appears, i.e. both heads):
$$E=\{HH\},\qquad n(E)=1$$

**Step 3 — the event $F$** (no head appears, i.e. both tails):
$$F=\{TT\},\qquad n(F)=1$$

**Step 4 — the intersection:** $E$ and $F$ cannot happen together:
$$E\cap F=\varnothing,\qquad n(E\cap F)=0$$

**Step 5 — conditional probability:**
$$P\left(\frac EF\right)=\frac{P(E\cap F)}{P(F)}=\frac{n(E\cap F)}{n(F)}=\frac01=0$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac EF\right)=0$$

**Interpretation:** 'no head appears' forces both coins to show tails, and then 'no tail appears' is impossible. The two events are mutually exclusive, so conditioning on one rules the other out completely — hence probability $0$. (Note also $P(E)=\dfrac14$, $P(F)=\dfrac14$, so $P(E\cap F)=0\neq\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac14=P(E)P(F)$: the events are **not** independent.)

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,\sin^{-1}x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — substitute** $t=\sin^{-1}x$. Then
$$\frac{dt}{dx}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\ \Rightarrow\ dt=\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$$

which is exactly the rest of the integrand.

**Step 2 — the integral becomes elementary:**
$$\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\sin^{-1}x}dx=\int\frac{dt}{t}=\log\left|t\right|+C$$

**Step 3 — restore $t=\sin^{-1}x$:**
$$\therefore\ \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\sin^{-1}x}=\log\left|\sin^{-1}x\right|+C$$

**Check by differentiating** (chain rule, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$):
$$\frac{d}{dx}\log\left(\sin^{-1}x\right)=\frac{1}{\sin^{-1}x}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\ ✓$$

**Range note:** for $x\in(0,1)$ we have $\sin^{-1}x\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, so the modulus signs may be dropped and the answer written $\log\left(\sin^{-1}x\right)+C$.

questions.question: Prove that $f(x)=\begin{cases}x,&\text{if }x\le1\\ 5,&\text{if }x>1\end{cases}$ is not continuous at $x=1$.
questions.answer:
For continuity at $x=1$ we need
$$\lim_{x\to1^{-}}f(x)=f(1)=\lim_{x\to1^{+}}f(x)$$

**Left-hand limit** (branch $x\le1$):
$$\lim_{x\to1^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to1}x=1$$

**Value at the point:** $f(1)=1$ (the first branch includes $x=1$).

**Right-hand limit** (branch $x>1$):
$$\lim_{x\to1^{+}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to1}5=5$$

**Compare:**
$$\lim_{x\to1^{-}}f(x)=1\neq5=\lim_{x\to1^{+}}f(x)$$

$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is \textbf{not continuous} at }x=1\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Nature of the discontinuity:** this is a **jump discontinuity** (discontinuity of the first kind) — both one-sided limits exist and are finite, but they differ. The jump has magnitude $5-1=4$. The graph is the line $y=x$ up to and including $x=1$, then a horizontal line $y=5$ for $x>1$, leaving a gap at the height $4$.

questions.question: Find the interval in which the function $f(x)=10-6x-2x^{2}$ is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — differentiate:**
$$f(x)=10-6x-2x^{2}$$
$$f'(x)=-6-4x=-2\left(2x+3\right)$$

**Step 2 — the critical point** from $f'(x)=0$:
$$2x+3=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=-\frac32$$

**Step 3 — sign of $f'(x)=-2\left(2x+3\right)$.** The factor $-2$ is negative, so the sign is *opposite* to that of $2x+3$:

| Interval | $2x+3$ | $f'(x)$ | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\left(-\infty,-\dfrac32\right)$ | $-$ | $+$ | increasing |
| $\left(-\dfrac32,\infty\right)$ | $+$ | $-$ | decreasing |

$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is strictly increasing on }\left(-\infty,-\dfrac32\right)\ \text{and strictly decreasing on }\left(-\dfrac32,\infty\right)$$

**Geometric check:** completing the square,
$$f(x)=-2x^{2}-6x+10=-2\left(x+\frac32\right)^{2}+\frac{29}{2}$$
so the graph is a downward parabola with vertex at $\left(-\dfrac32,\dfrac{29}{2}\right)$ — rising to the vertex, then falling ✓. The maximum value is $\dfrac{29}{2}=14.5$.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int\frac{2x-3}{x^{2}+6x+13}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — split the numerator into a multiple of the denominator's derivative plus a constant.** The derivative is $2x+6$, so write
$$2x-3=A\left(2x+6\right)+B$$

Comparing coefficients:
$$2A=2\ \Rightarrow\ A=1$$
$$6A+B=-3\ \Rightarrow\ B=-3-6=-9$$

$$\therefore\ 2x-3=\left(2x+6\right)-9$$

**Step 2 — split the integral:**
$$I=\int\frac{2x+6}{x^{2}+6x+13}\,dx-9\int\frac{dx}{x^{2}+6x+13}$$

**Step 3 — the first piece** is a logarithm (put $t=x^{2}+6x+13$, $dt=(2x+6)dx$):
$$\int\frac{2x+6}{x^{2}+6x+13}\,dx=\log\left|x^{2}+6x+13\right|$$

**Step 4 — the second piece.** Complete the square:
$$x^{2}+6x+13=\left(x+3\right)^{2}+4=\left(x+3\right)^{2}+2^{2}$$

so with $a=2$, $u=x+3$:
$$\int\frac{dx}{\left(x+3\right)^{2}+4}=\frac12\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+3}{2}\right)$$

**Step 5 — combine:**
$$\therefore\ I=\log\left(x^{2}+6x+13\right)-\frac92\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+3}{2}\right)+C$$

**The modulus signs may be dropped** because $x^{2}+6x+13=(x+3)^{2}+4\ge4>0$ for all $x$.

**Check by differentiating:** the first term gives $\dfrac{2x+6}{x^{2}+6x+13}$; the second gives $-\dfrac92\cdot\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{4}}\cdot\dfrac12=-\dfrac{9}{x^{2}+6x+13}$. Together $\dfrac{2x+6-9}{x^{2}+6x+13}=\dfrac{2x-3}{x^{2}+6x+13}$ ✓.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^{5}x}{\sin^{5}x+\cos^{5}x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let
$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^{5}x}{\sin^{5}x+\cos^{5}x}\,dx\qquad\ldots(1)$$

**Step 1 — apply $x\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x$**, using $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)dx$. Under it $\sin x\to\cos x$ and $\cos x\to\sin x$:
$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^{5}x}{\cos^{5}x+\sin^{5}x}\,dx\qquad\ldots(2)$$

**Step 2 — add (1) and (2).** The denominators are identical and the numerators add to the denominator:
$$2I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^{5}x+\sin^{5}x}{\sin^{5}x+\cos^{5}x}\,dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}1\,dx$$

**Step 3 — evaluate:**
$$2I=\left[x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}=\frac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ I=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^{5}x}{\sin^{5}x+\cos^{5}x}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

**Generalisation:** for every positive function $f$,
$$\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{f(\cos x)}{f(\sin x)+f(\cos x)}dx=\frac{\pi}{4}$$
because the substitution merely swaps the two halves of the integrand. Setting $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ in the integrand gives $1$ and $0$, so $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is the natural 'average' — a good sanity check.

questions.question: Find the area enclosed by the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=a^{2}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — use symmetry.** The circle of radius $a$ centred at the origin is symmetric about both axes, so its total area is $4$ times the area in the first quadrant.

**Step 2 — the first-quadrant part** is bounded by $y=\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$ above, the $x$-axis below, from $x=0$ to $x=a$:
$$\frac{A}{4}=\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx$$

**Step 3 — evaluate** with $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}dx=\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}+\frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac xa$:
$$\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}dx=\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}+\frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac xa\right]_{0}^{a}$$
$$=\left(0+\frac{a^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-0=\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4}$$

**Step 4 — multiply by 4:**
$$A=4\cdot\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4}=\pi a^{2}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{area enclosed}=\pi a^{2}\ \text{sq. units}$$

**Alternative (quick) route:** the circle is the ellipse $\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{a^{2}}=1$ with semi-axes $a,a$, and the ellipse's area is $\pi\times(\text{semi-major})\times(\text{semi-minor})=\pi a\cdot a=\pi a^{2}$ ✓ — the same result, which is the standard check.

questions.question: Solve the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y^{2}}{xy-x^{2}}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — check homogeneity.** Numerator $y^{2}$ has degree 2; denominator $xy-x^{2}$ also has degree 2. So the equation is homogeneous, and the substitution $\dfrac yx=v$ applies.

Divide numerator and denominator by $x^{2}$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(y/x)^{2}}{(y/x)-1}=\frac{v^{2}}{v-1}\qquad\ldots(1)$$

**Step 2 — substitute $y=vx$**, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$:
$$v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{v^{2}}{v-1}$$

**Step 3 — isolate $x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$:**
$$x\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{v^{2}}{v-1}-v=\frac{v^{2}-v^{2}+v}{v-1}=\frac{v}{v-1}$$

**Step 4 — separate the variables:**
$$\frac{v-1}{v}\,dv=\frac{dx}{x}$$
$$\left(1-\frac1v\right)dv=\frac{dx}{x}$$

**Step 5 — integrate:**
$$v-\log\left|v\right|=\log\left|x\right|+C$$

**Step 6 — restore $v=\dfrac yx$:**
$$\frac yx-\log\left|\frac yx\right|=\log\left|x\right|+C$$

Use $\log\left|\dfrac yx\right|=\log|y|-\log|x|$:
$$\frac yx-\log|y|+\log|x|=\log|x|+C$$
$$\frac yx=\log|y|+C$$

$$\therefore\ \frac yx-\log|y|=C\quad\text{equivalently}\quad y=x\left(\log|y|+C\right)$$

which is the required general solution.

**Check by differentiation** of $y=x\left(\log y+C\right)$: write $F(x,y)=\dfrac yx-\log y-C=0$. Then
$$F_{x}=-\frac{y}{x^{2}},\qquad F_{y}=\frac1x-\frac1y=\frac{y-x}{xy}$$
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{F_x}{F_y}=\frac{y/x^{2}}{(y-x)/(xy)}=\frac{y^{2}}{x(y-x)}=\frac{y^{2}}{xy-x^{2}}\ ✓$$
— exactly the given equation.

questions.question: Find the angle between the lines $\dfrac x1=\dfrac y0=\dfrac z3$ and $\dfrac x4=\dfrac y5=\dfrac z0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — direction ratios.**
$$\vec b_{1}=(1,\ 0,\ 3),\qquad \vec b_{2}=(4,\ 5,\ 0)$$

**Step 2 — the angle formula:**
$$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}}{\left|\vec b_{1}\right|\left|\vec b_{2}\right|}$$

**Numerator:**
$$\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}=(1)(4)+(0)(5)+(3)(0)=4+0+0=4$$

**Magnitudes:**
$$\left|\vec b_{1}\right|=\sqrt{1+0+9}=\sqrt{10},\qquad \left|\vec b_{2}\right|=\sqrt{16+25+0}=\sqrt{41}$$

**Step 3 — compute:**
$$\cos\theta=\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}\cdot\sqrt{41}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{410}}$$

$$\therefore\ \theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{410}}\right)\approx\cos^{-1}(0.1975)\approx78.6^{\circ}$$

**Sense check:** the first line lies entirely in a plane of constant $y$ (its $y$-direction ratio is $0$), while the second lies in a plane of constant $z$ — the two directions are nearly perpendicular, and indeed $78.6^{\circ}$ is close to $90^{\circ}$ ✓. Also $\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{410}}\approx\dfrac{4}{20.25}\approx0.197$.

questions.question: Find the area enclosed by the ellipse $\dfrac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\dfrac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — use symmetry.** The ellipse is symmetric about both axes, so its area is $4$ times the first-quadrant part.

**Step 2 — the upper branch in the first quadrant.** From the equation,
$$\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1-\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ y=\frac ba\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$$

so
$$\frac{A}{4}=\int_{0}^{a}\frac ba\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx$$

**Step 3 — evaluate the standard integral:**
$$\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx=\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}+\frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac xa\right]_{0}^{a}=\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4}$$

**Step 4 — multiply:**
$$A=4\cdot\frac ba\cdot\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4}=\pi ab$$

$$\therefore\ \text{area enclosed by the ellipse}=\pi ab\ \text{sq. units}$$

**Sanity checks:** for $a=b$ the ellipse is a circle and the formula gives $\pi a^{2}$ ✓; and for $a=2$, $b=1$ it gives $2\pi\approx6.28$, while the circumscribing rectangle $4\times2=8$ is larger ✓ and the inscribed rhombus has area $2ab=4$, smaller ✓ — so $\pi ab$ sits sensibly between them.

questions.topic: System of Equations by Matrix Method
questions.question: Using matrix method solve the following system of equations: $4x+3y+2z=60$, $x+2y+3z=45$, $6x+2y+3z=70$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — write as $AX=B$:**
$$\begin{bmatrix}4&3&2\\ 1&2&3\\ 6&2&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}60\\ 45\\ 70\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — the determinant:**
$$|A|=4\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\ 2&3\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}1&3\\ 6&3\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\ 6&2\end{vmatrix}$$
$$=4(6-6)-3(3-18)+2(2-12)$$
$$=0-3(-15)+2(-10)=45-20=25$$

Since $|A|=25\neq0$, the system has a unique solution $X=A^{-1}B$.

**Step 3 — the cofactors:**
$$C_{11}=+\left(6-6\right)=0\qquad C_{12}=-\left(3-18\right)=15\qquad C_{13}=+\left(2-12\right)=-10$$
$$C_{21}=-\left(9-4\right)=-5\qquad C_{22}=+\left(12-12\right)=0\qquad C_{23}=-\left(8-18\right)=10$$
$$C_{31}=+\left(9-4\right)=5\qquad C_{32}=-\left(12-2\right)=-10\qquad C_{33}=+\left(8-3\right)=5$$

**Step 4 — the adjoint** (cofactor matrix transposed):
$$\text{adj}\,A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-5&5\\ 15&0&-10\\ -10&10&5\end{bmatrix}$$

$$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{25}\begin{bmatrix}0&-5&5\\ 15&0&-10\\ -10&10&5\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 5 — multiply by $B$** (working with $25X=(\text{adj}A)B$ to avoid fractions):

$$25x=0(60)+(-5)(45)+5(70)=0-225+350=125\ \Rightarrow\ x=5$$
$$25y=15(60)+0(45)+(-10)(70)=900-700=200\ \Rightarrow\ y=8$$
$$25z=(-10)(60)+10(45)+5(70)=-600+450+350=200\ \Rightarrow\ z=8$$

$$\therefore\ x=5,\quad y=8,\quad z=8$$

**Check in the original equations:**
$$4(5)+3(8)+2(8)=20+24+16=60\ ✓$$
$$5+2(8)+3(8)=5+16+24=45\ ✓$$
$$6(5)+2(8)+3(8)=30+16+24=70\ ✓$$

**Alternative check on $A^{-1}$:** $A\cdot\text{adj}A=|A|I$, e.g. first row of $A$ times first column of adj: $4(0)+3(15)+2(-10)=45-20=25=|A|$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of the given function $f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9x-8$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — first derivative:**
$$f'(x)=3x^{2}-12x+9=3\left(x^{2}-4x+3\right)=3(x-1)(x-3)$$

**Step 2 — second derivative:**
$$f''(x)=6x-12$$

**Step 3 — critical points** from $f'(x)=0$:
$$x=1,\qquad x=3$$

**Step 4 — classify each.**

*At $x=1$:*
$$f''(1)=6-12=-6<0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local maximum}$$
$$f(1)=1-6+9-8=-4$$

*At $x=3$:*
$$f''(3)=18-12=6>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local minimum}$$
$$f(3)=27-54+27-8=-8$$

| $x$ | $f''(x)$ | nature | value |
|---|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $-6$ | maximum | $-4$ |
| $3$ | $6$ | minimum | $-8$ |

$$\therefore\ \text{maximum value}=-4\ \text{at }x=1;\qquad \text{minimum value}=-8\ \text{at }x=3$$

**These are local extrema only.** Because $f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9x-8\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$ and $\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$, the function has **no absolute** maximum or minimum on $\mathbb{R}$. Between the critical points it falls from $-4$ to $-8$, then rises again — the classic 'rise, fall, rise' shape of a cubic with positive leading coefficient.

questions.question: Find the shortest distance between the lines $\vec r=\left(\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k\right)+\lambda\left(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)$ and $\vec r=\left(2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k\right)+\mu\left(2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k\right)$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the data:**
$$\vec a_{1}=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k,\qquad \vec b_{1}=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$$
$$\vec a_{2}=2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k,\qquad \vec b_{2}=2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$$

For skew lines,
$$d=\frac{\left|\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\cdot\left(\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right)\right|}{\left|\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right|}$$

**Step 2 — a vector joining the two given points:**
$$\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}=\left(2-1\right)\hat i+\left(-1-2\right)\hat j+\left(-1-1\right)\hat k=\hat i-3\hat j-2\hat k$$

**Step 3 — the cross product of the directions:**
$$\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 1&-1&1\\ 2&1&2\end{vmatrix}$$
$$=\hat i\left[(-1)(2)-(1)(1)\right]-\hat j\left[(1)(2)-(1)(2)\right]+\hat k\left[(1)(1)-(-1)(2)\right]$$
$$=\hat i(-2-1)-\hat j(2-2)+\hat k(1+2)=-3\hat i+0\hat j+3\hat k$$

$${\left|\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right|}=\sqrt{9+0+9}=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt2$$

**Step 4 — the scalar triple product:**
$$\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\cdot\left(\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right)=(1)(-3)+(-3)(0)+(-2)(3)=-3-6=-9$$

**Step 5 — the distance:**
$$d=\frac{\left|-9\right|}{3\sqrt2}=\frac{9}{3\sqrt2}=\frac{3}{\sqrt2}=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}$$

$$\therefore\ d=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\approx2.121\ \text{units}$$

**The lines are genuinely skew** since $d\neq0$; and $\vec b_{1},\vec b_{2}$ are non-parallel (their cross product is non-zero), so the formula used is the right one.

**Cross-check by the alternative formula:** $d=\dfrac{\left|\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\cdot\vec n\right|}{\left|\vec n\right|}$ with $\vec n=\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}=3(-\hat i+\hat k)$ reduces to $\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}$ ✓.

questions.question: Solve the following LPP graphically: Maximise $Z=x+y$ subject to constraints $2x+y\le50$, $x+2y\le40$, $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — draw the boundary lines.**

**Line 1:** $2x+y=50$; intercepts $(25,0)$ and $(0,50)$.

**Line 2:** $x+2y=40$; intercepts $(40,0)$ and $(0,20)$.

Both pass the origin test ($0\le50$, $0\le40$), so the feasible side is the one containing the origin, and with $x,y\ge0$ the feasible region is a quadrilateral in the first quadrant.

**Step 2 — find the corner points.**

- $O(0,0)$ — the origin, feasible.
- Where line 1 meets the $x$-axis: $y=0\Rightarrow2x=50\Rightarrow x=25$: $\;(25,0)$; check line 2: $25\le40$ ✓ so it is feasible.
- Where line 2 meets the $x$-axis: $y=0\Rightarrow x=40$; but line 1 gives $80>50$ ✗, so $(40,0)$ is **not** feasible.
- Where line 1 meets the $y$-axis: $x=0\Rightarrow y=50$; line 2 gives $100>40$ ✗, so $(0,50)$ is **not** feasible.
- Where line 2 meets the $y$-axis: $x=0\Rightarrow2y=40\Rightarrow y=20$: $\;(0,20)$, feasible since $20\le50$ ✓.
- Where the two lines cross: solve
$$2x+y=50,\qquad x+2y=40$$
Multiply the second by $2$: $2x+4y=80$; subtract the first: $3y=30\Rightarrow y=10$; then $x=40-2(10)=20$:
$$C(20,10)$$

So the feasible polygon has vertices
$$O(0,0),\quad (25,0),\quad C(20,10),\quad (0,20)$$

**Step 3 — evaluate $Z=x+y$ at every corner.**

| Vertex | $Z=x+y$ |
|---|---|
| $O(0,0)$ | $0$ |
| $(25,0)$ | $25$ |
| $C(20,10)$ | $30$ |
| $(0,20)$ | $20$ |

**Step 4 — conclusion.** The largest value is $30$, attained at $C(20,10)$:
$$\therefore\ Z_{\max}=30\quad\text{at}\quad x=20,\ y=10$$

**Feasibility check of $C$:** $2(20)+10=50\le50$ ✓ (tight) and $20+2(10)=40\le40$ ✓ (tight) — both constraints bind there, the typical signature of an optimal vertex.

**Geometric reading:** $Z=x+y$ has level lines of slope $-1$, which is *flatter* than either boundary (slopes $-2$ and $-\tfrac12$), so the furthest such line touching the region grazes it at the corner $C$ ✓.

questions.question: Two bags I and II are given. Bag I contains $3$ red and $4$ black balls while another bag II contains $5$ red and $6$ black balls. One ball is drawn at random from one of the bags and it is found to be red. Find the probability that it was drawn from bag II.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the two sources (equally likely).**
$$P\left(E_{1}\right)=P\left(\text{Bag I}\right)=\frac12,\qquad P\left(E_{2}\right)=P\left(\text{Bag II}\right)=\frac12$$

**Step 2 — the conditional probabilities of a red ball.**

Bag I: $3$ red out of $3+4=7$ balls:
$$P\left(\frac{R}{E_{1}}\right)=\frac37$$

Bag II: $5$ red out of $5+6=11$ balls:
$$P\left(\frac{R}{E_{2}}\right)=\frac{5}{11}$$

**Step 3 — Bayes' theorem:**
$$P\left(\frac{E_{2}}{R}\right)=\frac{P\left(E_{2}\right)P\left(\frac{R}{E_{2}}\right)}{P\left(E_{1}\right)P\left(\frac{R}{E_{1}}\right)+P\left(E_{2}\right)P\left(\frac{R}{E_{2}}\right)}$$

The common factor $\dfrac12$ cancels:
$$=\frac{\dfrac{5}{11}}{\dfrac37+\dfrac{5}{11}}=\frac{\dfrac{5}{11}}{\dfrac{33+35}{77}}=\frac{5/11}{68/77}$$

$$=\frac{5}{11}\cdot\frac{77}{68}=\frac{5\cdot7}{68}=\frac{35}{68}$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac{E_{2}}{R}\right)=\frac{35}{68}\approx0.515$$

**Interpretation:** Bag II has the slightly higher proportion of reds ($\dfrac{5}{11}\approx0.4545$ versus $\dfrac37\approx0.4286$), so drawing a red ball raises the chance that it came from bag II — but only from $0.500$ to $0.515$ ✓. The complementary posterior is $\dfrac{33}{68}\approx0.485$, and $\dfrac{35}{68}+\dfrac{33}{68}=1$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the local maximum and local minimum values of the given function: $f(x)=3x^{4}+4x^{3}-12x^{2}+12$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — first derivative:**
$$f'(x)=12x^{3}+12x^{2}-24x=12x\left(x^{2}+x-2\right)=12x(x+2)(x-1)$$

**Step 2 — second derivative:**
$$f''(x)=36x^{2}+24x-24$$

**Step 3 — critical points** from $f'(x)=0$:
$$x=0,\qquad x=-2,\qquad x=1$$

**Step 4 — test each critical point.**

*At $x=0$:*
$$f''(0)=-24<0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local maximum}$$
$$f(0)=0+0-0+12=12$$

*At $x=-2$:*
$$f''(-2)=36(4)+24(-2)-24=144-48-24=72>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local minimum}$$
$$f(-2)=3(16)+4(-8)-12(4)+12=48-32-48+12=-20$$

*At $x=1$:*
$$f''(1)=36+24-24=36>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local minimum}$$
$$f(1)=3+4-12+12=7$$

| $x$ | $f''(x)$ | nature | value |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0$ | $-24$ | local maximum | $12$ |
| $-2$ | $72$ | local minimum | $-20$ |
| $1$ | $36$ | local minimum | $7$ |

$$\therefore\ \text{local maximum}=12\ \text{at }x=0;\qquad \text{local minima}=-20\ \text{at }x=-2\ \text{and }7\ \text{at }x=1$$

**Shape check:** $f$ is a quartic with positive leading coefficient, so it rises to $+\infty$ at both ends and can have at most one local maximum — which is exactly the single maximum at $x=0$, sitting between the two minima ✓. Reading left to right: $f$ falls to $-20$ at $x=-2$, rises to $12$ at $x=0$, falls to $7$ at $x=1$, then rises forever.
